assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population administrative data transformed the measurement of intergenerational mobility and made its geographic and institutional variation a central empirical object.
assessment.attribution: Chetty, Hendren, and Friedman are central to the linked-data research program; the broader collaboration makes exact division of credit difficult.
assessment.maturity: The findings and measurement approach have been extensively developed, replicated in related settings, and influential in research and public debate.
uncertainties: Whether the empirical measurement program constitutes one sufficiently bounded discovery for a prize.
The appropriate treatment of additional collaborators in attribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work reshaped understanding of how trade and technological change alter local labour demand, employment, and wage inequality.
assessment.attribution: Autor, Dorn, and Hanson form a clear core for the trade-shock contribution, while Katz is important to adjacent work on technology and inequality.
assessment.maturity: The research has generated a large subsequent literature and its empirical implications have remained highly consequential.
uncertainties: Trade and automation mechanisms are intertwined in the wider literature.
The durability and generality of local-adjustment estimates remain active research questions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The revival of monopsony as a practical framework changed the analysis of wage setting, employer power, and labour-market policy.
assessment.attribution: Manning supplied foundational modern analysis; Naidu is a leading contributor to the subsequent empirical and institutional research.
assessment.maturity: The framework now organizes a broad mature literature and has clear relevance for wage and competition policy.
uncertainties: Attribution spans older theory and a large, still-expanding empirical literature.
The magnitude of monopsony power varies substantially across labour markets.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Correspondence and audit designs provided unusually direct evidence on labour-market discrimination and established an enduring empirical template.
assessment.attribution: Bertrand and Mullainathan are the clearest joint attribution for the landmark correspondence-study contribution; Charles is an important broader contributor.
assessment.maturity: The approach has been widely applied across countries and groups, with substantial influence on labour economics.
uncertainties: Audit estimates identify responses to applications, not every channel through which discrimination operates.
The contribution builds on an older audit-study tradition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Research on fetal and early-childhood conditions made the dynamic origins of health, education, and later economic outcomes central to applied economics.
assessment.attribution: Currie, Almond, and Cunha represent complementary causal and developmental contributions, though the broader field has many essential contributors.
assessment.maturity: Evidence accumulated over decades and has materially shaped health, education, and social-policy research.
uncertainties: The candidate combines several related mechanisms and empirical approaches.
Long-run causal interpretation can depend on setting-specific identification.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The integration of insurance-market theory with credible measurement substantially improved understanding of selection, pricing, and welfare.
assessment.attribution: Finkelstein, Einav, and Salanie are all central to connecting adverse-selection theory to empirical insurance markets.
assessment.maturity: The methods and findings are established and influential across health, credit, and other insurance settings.
uncertainties: The appropriate balance between foundational theory and later empirical implementation is contestable.
Selection patterns vary across institutional environments.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The reconstruction of long-run income, wealth, and offshore-wealth distributions transformed the empirical basis for studying inequality.
assessment.attribution: Piketty, Saez, and Zucman are leading architects of the linked measurement program, though it rests on extensive archival and international collaboration.
assessment.maturity: The data and associated research have had deep, sustained influence across public economics and political economy.
uncertainties: Measurement choices for wealth, capital income, and offshore holdings remain debated.
A prize would need to distinguish data construction from contested broader interpretations.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Empirical work on taxable-income responses gave optimal-tax analysis a more credible behavioural and administrative-data foundation.
assessment.attribution: Slemrod provided foundational work on behavioural tax responses, while Saez and Chetty advanced empirical measurement and policy design.
assessment.maturity: The elasticity of taxable income and related administrative-data methods are now central to modern public-finance analysis.
uncertainties: Estimated elasticities depend on tax-system details, avoidance opportunities, and modelling choices.
The contribution overlaps with broader literatures on inequality and tax administration.
